name: Photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT)
lead: ALA-PDT is a clinic procedure in which a dermatologist applies aminolevulinic acid (ALA) to the skin and then shines a light of a matching wavelength on it. Cells in the treated area turn ALA into a light-sensitive compound, protoporphyrin IX, and the light then triggers reactive oxygen species that destroy the targeted cells.[1][2] People look into it for visible skin concerns: inflamed, stubborn or severe acne, sun-damaged skin with rough sun spots (actinic keratoses), and, off label, general facial rejuvenation.[2][3]

Because the effect is confined to the area that is both sensitised and illuminated, the treatment can be directed at the face, and the skin typically clears and renews after the sunburn-like reaction settles, usually over several weeks.[2] DermNet lists acne and facial rejuvenation among the off-label or investigational uses, while actinic keratosis, Bowen disease and superficial basal cell carcinoma are the approved ones.[2]

For acne, a 2016 systematic review described PDT as a safe and effective treatment, while one phase II trial found improvement that was not better than blue or violet light alone.[1] A small randomized trial compared ALA with its methyl ester (MAL) for inflamed facial acne.[4] A 2022 network meta-analysis of acne treatments covered physical treatments, including light-based ones, alongside drugs.[5] Redness, burning, pain and light sensitivity for about a day are the main reported side effects.[1][2]

Light activates it and destroys targeted cells

angle.text: ALA-PDT is used in dermatology clinics to treat inflamed acne and sun-damaged patches on the face, and some clinics offer it for rejuvenation. Users go to it when they want clearer, smoother-looking facial skin, accepting a sunburn-like reaction that heals over a few weeks.

paras: A photosensitizer collects in the target tissue and is activated by light, passing energy to oxygen and producing singlet oxygen and other reactive species that damage cell membranes and proteins; because damage occurs only where light is applied, the effect stays localised.[1] ALA is a prodrug: it is the first compound in the body's heme-making pathway, and applying extra of it makes protoporphyrin IX accumulate faster than cells convert it to heme.[6] The compound peaks within hours and clears in about a day, which limits how long skin stays light-sensitive.[1]
In acne, proposed mechanisms include damage to the oil-producing sebaceous glands and to acne-associated bacteria, though the details are still being studied.[5]

A 2009 review of PDT for localized infections noted numerous clinical acne studies but said the role of microbial killing in the clinical benefit is unclear, consistent with the view that effects on sebaceous glands and inflammation also contribute.[13]

According to DermNet, the skin may be lightly scraped or needled to help the drug penetrate, the photosensitiser is left on for about 3 to 6 hours, and the area is then illuminated with laser or non-laser light or with daylight. Artificial-light sessions usually last 5 to 45 minutes, daylight sessions about 2 hours, and a second session may be given 7 to 10 days later.[2] A local anaesthetic spray can ease discomfort, and the area is covered afterwards to block further light.[2]
Treated skin develops a sunburn-like reaction, with the surface typically healing within 4 to 8 weeks.[2]

Daylight PDT uses natural daylight for about two hours instead of an artificial lamp, which DermNet describes as free and convenient but unreliable in some locations and seasons.[2] The treated area is covered with a dressing afterwards to block further light exposure, and DermNet notes that recent evidence suggests topical PDT may work better after a 7-day course of high-dose oral vitamin D.[2]

PDT has been studied mainly for severe or inflammatory acne. Early trial results suggested a benefit in severe cases, and a 2016 systematic review called it safe and effective.[1] In the trial that compared ALA-PDT with MAL-PDT, 15 patients with at least 12 inflamed facial lesions were treated and followed for treatment effect and tolerability.[4]

Actinic keratoses are rough, scaly sun-damage patches, and ALA-PDT is an approved treatment for them. Facial rejuvenation is listed as an off-label use.[2] A 2025 phase 1 registration studied activating an ALA product with a broadband light device for actinic keratoses and photodamage.[7]

Around 1900, Oscar Raab and Hermann von Tappeiner found that light and oxygen were needed for dyes to kill cells, and von Tappeiner named the effect photodynamic action.[1] In 1978 Thomas Dougherty's group reported treating 113 skin and subcutaneous tumours, with total or partial resolution in 111, and Photofrin became the first PDT agent approved for clinical use, in Canada in 1993.[1] Topical ALA-based PDT for skin conditions developed from this work.[8]

The photosensitiser in this procedure, aminolevulinic acid, is an endogenous amino acid that starts the porphyrin pathway leading to heme in mammals, and it is sold under names including Levulan, NatuALA and Ameluz. It is prescription-only in Canada, the US and the EU, and its other medical uses include fluorescence visualisation in bladder cancer and in glioma surgery, which the FDA approved for glioma in 2017.[3]

Wikipedia's history places the roots of light therapy in Niels Finsen's filtered-light treatment of lupus vulgaris, recognised with the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and notes that von Tappeiner's group ran an early photodynamic trial in facial basal cell carcinoma using eosin, with total resolution in four of six patients.[1] In 1913 Meyer-Betz injected himself with haematoporphyrin and developed sun sensitivity, an early demonstration of the drawback shared by photosensitisers.[1] The FDA approved porfimer sodium in 1994 for esophageal cancer, and the FDA now lists actinic keratosis among approved PDT indications.[1]

A 1998 review by Dougherty and colleagues surveyed 25 years of clinical PDT, and later reviews list ALA and its esters (methyl aminolevulinate, hexaminolevulinate) as approved precursors of protoporphyrin IX, noting approval of PDT for acne vulgaris in some jurisdictions.[13]

The main side effect is skin photosensitivity, which for ALA lasts about 24 hours.[1][2] DermNet lists stinging or burning, redness, swelling, itching, crusting, peeling and blistering, and rarely skin infection; a loss of pigment can occur and may be permanent.[2] In acne treatment, marked redness and moderate to severe pain or burning have been reported.[1]
DermNet says scarring is usually minimal but can occasionally be moderate, and that the treated lesion may blister and ulcerate as cells die, taking several weeks to heal.[2]

Acne, ALA versus MAL: a 2006 randomised, investigator-blinded, paired split-face trial in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology treated 15 adults and adolescents with at least 12 inflamed facial acne lesions, with MAL on one side of the face and ALA on the other. At 12 weeks, inflammatory lesions had fallen 59% from baseline, and effectiveness did not differ significantly between the two photosensitisers. All patients had moderate to severe pain during illumination and developed redness, pustular eruptions and exfoliation; these were more severe and more uniform on the ALA side, and the authors concluded that ALA-PDT caused more prolonged and severe adverse effects. They noted that the small number of participants calls for cautious interpretation.[4]

Acne, reviews: a 2016 systematic review called PDT safe and effective for acne, while a phase II trial found it no better than blue or violet light alone.[1] A network meta-analysis of randomised trials in acne vulgaris compared topical, oral, physical and combined treatments in mild-to-moderate and moderate-to-severe acne.[5]
Pigment disorders: a 2019 randomised trial published as a letter in Dermatologic Surgery examined microneedling combined with photodynamic therapy in vitiligo.[12]
Photodamage: a 2025 phase 1 registration studied activating an ALA product with a broadband light device for actinic keratoses and photodamage in 10 people.[7]

Skin cancer and precancer: a 2001 open study examined ALA-PDT for large or multiple patches of Bowen disease and basal cell carcinoma, and a 2004 review covered laser and PDT for non-melanoma skin cancer.[8][9] Registered trials cover actinic keratosis, including a phase 3 field-treatment study and daylight-PDT studies.[10][11] These concern skin cancer rather than appearance.

PDT appears in dermatology practice mainly as a treatment for actinic keratoses and superficial skin cancers. DermNet lists acne and facial rejuvenation among off-label uses, so how a clinic uses it for appearance varies.[2] Patients describe or are told to expect a sunburn-like reaction that heals over several weeks, and the treated area must be kept out of light for about a day.[1][2] No community discussion specific to ALA-PDT was found in forums.

Clinics also use blue and red light panels, intense pulsed light, lasers and chemical peels for acne and photodamage; ALA-PDT is sometimes combined with microneedling, which a 2019 randomized trial examined in vitiligo.[12] Wikipedia notes that topical ALA has also been investigated for psoriasis, Bowen disease and hirsutism in phase II/III work.[1]

lore.intro: ALA-PDT appears in clinic marketing and dermatology reviews more than in forum threads; the claims below are those made by providers and in reviews.

claims.believers: Clinics and some reviews describe benefit for severe or inflammatory acne, with improvement lasting after the sunburn-like reaction heals.[1]
claims.experts: A 2006 split-face trial reported 59 percent fewer inflamed lesions at 12 weeks in 15 patients, and a phase II trial found no advantage over blue or violet light alone.[4][1]

claims.believers: Providers offer it for rough, sun-spotted skin and facial rejuvenation, where treating actinic keratoses also smooths texture.[2]
claims.experts: DermNet lists rejuvenation as off-label; actinic keratosis is an approved use, and a small 2025 phase 1 study examined photodamage.[2][7]

claims.claim: Daylight activation gives similar results with less pain
claims.believers: Daylight sessions of about two hours are promoted as convenient and gentler.[2]
claims.experts: DermNet describes daylight PDT as free and convenient but unreliable in some places and seasons; registered trials compare it with lamp-based PDT.[2][11]

claims.believers: Some assume the natural prodrug is milder.
claims.experts: In the 2006 trial, adverse effects were more severe and more uniform on the ALA side, with similar effectiveness.[4]

claims.believers: Social posts sometimes show quick peeling.
claims.experts: DermNet says surface healing usually takes 4 to 8 weeks, with light avoidance for about a day and possible blistering or lasting pigment loss.[2]

card.summary: Photosensitizer plus light for severe acne; some trials and a review are positive, but results are mixed and treatment is painful.
card.note: Clinician-administered; pain, redness and photosensitivity are common.

quick.overview:
ALA-PDT applies aminolevulinic acid to the skin and then light, which kills targeted cells. It is established for actinic keratosis and some skin cancers and has been studied for severe acne.

A 2016 review called it safe and effective for acne, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue or violet light alone.
quick.mechanism: ALA makes cells accumulate protoporphyrin IX, which on light exposure produces reactive oxygen species that damage the treated cells.
quick.risks: Marked redness, moderate to severe pain, burning and photosensitivity are reported. It is performed by clinicians.
